the-mad-podcast-with-matt-turck.name: The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck
the-mad-podcast-with-matt-turck.bio: Podcast: Stripe's AI Chief: How AI Agents Will Buy, Sell, and Pay

html_en:
Agentic commerce is moving from whiteboard theory to live infrastructure — and the friction, fraud, and trust challenges arriving with it are more complex than anyone anticipated.

The Agent Economy Has a Plumbing Problem

A year ago, conversations about AI agents buying and selling things on your behalf were largely speculative. Today, according to this week's episode of The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck, the infrastructure is live, the early partners are named, and the hard lessons are accumulating fast. Emily Sands, head of data and AI at Stripe, offered one of the most grounded and detailed pictures yet of what agentic commerce actually looks like in the wild.

The core insight Sands brings is that "agent e-commerce" isn't a single thing — it's a spectrum. At one end, fully autonomous agents discover a service, evaluate it, and transact without any human in the loop. At the other, a shopper searches for running shoes inside an AI surface and sees a buy button alongside the answer. Both are real, both are growing, and both need new infrastructure.

"Whether we're talking about fully agent-led transactions with MPP or these very human-led purchases inside AI surfaces, there's just a new set of infrastructure that needs to work no matter where you are in the spectrum. Businesses need to be able to expose their products and their catalogs and their prices. Consumers need to be able to authorize agents to pay on their behalf. And then agents need to be able to safely execute that transaction." — Emily Sands, The MAD Podcast

Stripe has already shipped partnerships with Google (merchants selling inside AI Mode and the Gemini app), Microsoft and OpenAI (product discovery inside Copilot and ChatGPT), and Meta (powering checkout inside ads). Early brand adopters include Best Buy, Coach, and URBN. The platform side counts Shopify, Wix, BigCommerce, and Commerce Tools. In other words, this is no longer a proof-of-concept — it's becoming load-bearing infrastructure for how commerce works.

Levels of Autonomy — Sound Familiar?

Stripe has apparently developed its own framework for agentic commerce that maps almost directly onto the self-driving car autonomy levels that Tesla and Waymo made famous. Level one: the human makes all the decisions, the agent just executes the checkout. Level three: the agent selects, decides, and transacts largely on its own.

"On the consumer side, we're mostly hovering level two. People are delegating a little bit of the selection or leaning hard on the AI to help find the product, maybe a hint of level three — but we're not in a world where you're booking your summer vacation one-shotting it with an LLM." — Emily Sands, The MAD Podcast

The analogy is apt, and the implication is the same as it was for autonomous vehicles: the middle levels are the messy, complicated ones. Full autonomy is conceptually clean. Human-in-the-loop is safe. It's the hybrid zone — where the agent does some of the deciding — where liability, trust, and error attribution get genuinely hard. ChatGPT's Instant Checkout is cited as a current real-world example of that middle tier.

Sands frames the consumer trust question with refreshing clarity:

"When I go and ask my friends and family whether they'd be comfortable letting an agent buy things on their behalf, they usually jump straight to: is it gonna overspend, is it gonna buy the wrong thing, and can I stop it? And those are actually all legitimate concerns." — Emily Sands, The MAD Podcast

Her longer-term vision is more radical than a smarter checkout button, though. The end state she's watching for is the one where you tell your agent you have a $500 back-to-school budget, it already knows your kids' sizes and school supply lists, and it just... handles it. Or goes further: acts before you even ask.

Token Theft: The Most Under-Discussed Problem in AI

Perhaps the most striking segment of the conversation wasn't about commerce at all — it was about fraud. Sands describes what she calls the most under-discussed topic in the entire AI industry: the systematic theft of AI compute tokens at scale.

"Fraudsters have figured out that in AI, you actually don't really need to steal money or credentials. You can just steal tokens. And the scale of this actually shocked me when I looked at the data. More than one in six signups at AI companies are this kind of abuse." — Emily Sands, The MAD Podcast

She calls it the "dine and dash, but for tokens" — fraudulent accounts created specifically to consume inference capacity without paying. At one-in-six signups, this isn't an edge case; it's a structural tax on AI companies that is quietly eating into unit economics across the industry. Given how expensive frontier inference remains, the implications for any company running usage-based AI services are significant. This feels like a problem that will spawn its own category of security tooling before long.

The Bigger Picture: From Consumer to Operator

The conceptual shift Sands is most excited — and most deliberate — about is the move from thinking of AI agents as sophisticated personal shoppers to thinking of them as operators of businesses. The framing matters enormously.

"It's not Emily permissioning an agent to buy on her behalf. It's Emily has an agent who's tasked with running a business — and that includes buying some things and selling some things and making some profits. And that'll be the world that I would like to be talking about twelve months from now." — Emily Sands, The MAD Podcast

If that framing takes hold, the infrastructure requirements change dramatically. An agent running a business isn't just executing a single transaction — it's managing vendor relationships, cash flow, inventory decisions, and pricing strategy on an ongoing basis. Stripe's positioning, clearly, is to be the financial operating system underneath all of that. Whether the trust, regulatory, and liability frameworks can keep pace with the ambition is the open question that will define the next few years of this space.

html_zh:
AI代理正在悄然重塑商业基础设施——而与此同时，一种鲜为人知的新型欺诈正在侵蚀这个生态系统的根基。

🛒 代理商务的"自动驾驶分级"：从助手到自主买家

Stripe 数据与AI负责人 Emily Sands 近日做客 The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck，带来了目前关于"代理商务"（Agentic Commerce）最具体、最接地气的行业观察。她的核心观点是：代理参与商业交易并非只有一种形态，而是一个完整的光谱。

"在光谱的一端，是代理完全自主地发现服务、决定购买并独立完成交易——全程没有人工介入。另一端则是用户在AI界面里搜索'适合扁平足跑者的跑鞋'，AI给出答案，而这个答案越来越多地附带一个'购买'按钮。"
—— Emily Sands，Stripe 数据与AI负责人

这个框架让人想起自动驾驶的L1至L5分级。Stripe内部也确实采用了类似的层级划分：L1是人类主导决策、AI只负责执行支付；L3是代理帮你筛选商品、你点击确认；而最高级别，则是代理完全自主地替你经营一门生意。Emily坦言，目前消费者端大体停留在L2，"我们还没到一句话让LLM帮你订好整个暑假行程的阶段。"

在合作伙伴层面，Stripe的布局已颇具规模：与Google合作让商家直接在AI模式和Gemini应用内完成销售；与Microsoft、OpenAI合作让产品在Copilot和ChatGPT内可被发现；Meta则是另一个案例——Stripe为其广告内的一键结账提供支持。Wix、Shopify、Best Buy、Coach等平台和品牌也已在其"代理商务套件"上构建基础设施。

🚨 最被低估的AI安全议题：有人在"偷Token"

然而，这场代理商务革命的背后，潜伏着一个鲜有人讨论的安全危机。Emily将其称为整个AI领域"最被忽视的话题"。

"诈骗者已经发现，在AI领域，你其实不需要偷钱或偷凭证——你只需要偷Token。当我看到数据时，规模之大令我震惊：AI公司中，超过六分之一的新注册账户都是这类滥用行为。"
—— Emily Sands

她将这种行为生动地称为"Token版的餐厅逃单"（dine and dash，but for tokens）。用户注册账号、消耗算力资源，然后消失——AI公司承担成本，欺诈者获得免费推理能力。随着AI推理成本仍然高企，这一问题的经济破坏力不容小觑。

这也解释了为何"代理身份验证"和"代理授权"正成为基础设施建设的关键议题。当代理替你买东西，谁来验证这个代理的身份？谁来确保它不被滥用？这些问题的答案，将在很大程度上决定代理商务能走多远。

🔮 展望：当代理开始"经营企业"

对话最令人遐想的部分，是Emily描绘的那个稍远一些的未来：

"真正让我兴奋的，不是Emily授权一个代理替她买东西，而是——Emily有一个被委以重任的代理，它负责经营一门生意，包括买入一些东西、卖出一些东西、赚取一些利润。这才是我希望在十二个月后谈论的世界。"
—— Emily Sands

从"帮我找一双跑鞋"到"帮我经营一家公司"，这条路比想象中更近，但每一步都需要重新设计信任机制、授权边界和支付基础设施。Stripe的押注，正是这套新的经济底层协议。而对于所有在AI浪潮中寻找商业机会的从业者而言，Emily的判断值得认真对待：你的产品必须能被代理"发现"，否则你将在下一个十年的商业入口中缺席。
